title: The true yogi
hook: a true yogi is one who lives the Guru's teaching in ordinary life

segments.voice: Yesterday, the breath and the Name: the yogis trained the breath, and Nanak asked what it carries. Your line was the name in the breath. Which ordinary breath did you catch? Day one thousand one hundred forty-three.

What does a yogi look like? Ask around and the answers come quickly. Someone thin, on a mountain, cross-legged, far from phones and rent. Ash on the skin, maybe. Big earrings. A staff. Silence. The Siddhs in the Sidh Gosht looked something like that, and they had paid for it: they had left homes and families to live apart. Across from them sits Nanak, a man who, tradition says, went home to a family and fields. So a question hangs over the whole conversation. Where, then, is yoga found? Today: the true yogi.
screen: `A MOUNTAIN, ASH, A STAFF.` → `THE SIDDHS LEFT HOME.` → `WHERE IS YOGA FOUND?`

segments.voice: In the Sidh Gosht, Nanak's answer keeps returning to one figure: the Gurmukh, the person turned toward the Guru. In his answers, it is the Gurmukh who finds the way of yoga, through the Word. The old phrase for it is jog jugat, the method of yoga. Nanak doesn't throw the phrase out. He fills it with something else. A short hymn of his in Raga Suhi says it plainly, and it sits beside the Sidh Gosht like a summary. In paraphrase: yoga is not the patched coat, not the staff, not ash rubbed on the body. It isn't earrings or a shaved head or the blowing of a horn. Then the line that turns it: stay spotless in the middle of the soot. That is how the way of yoga is found. Soot. That's the picture. Not a clean mountain far away, but the smoky kitchen, the office, the crowded bus, the family argument. The test isn't whether you can stay pure where nothing touches you. It's whether you can stay clear in the place where everything does. That's why Sikh teaching honors the householder: someone who earns a living, cooks, cares for the young and the old, and keeps the Name through all of it. The yogis' discipline was real. Nanak doesn't call them lazy. He moves the discipline indoors, into the hours most people already live. A true yogi, in this reading, might be wiping a counter right now. Or waiting in a slow checkout line, steady. The coat and the staff aren't the point. The way you do the next ordinary thing is.
screen: `THE GURMUKH FINDS THE WAY.` · `NOT THE COAT, NOT THE STAFF.` · `SPOTLESS IN THE MIDDLE OF THE SOOT.` · `THE DISCIPLINE MOVES INDOORS.` · then, large: `YOGA IN DAILY LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one ordinary thing well. Pick something close by: a cup to wash, a shirt to fold, a drawer to close properly, a plant to water. Take your time. Feel the weight of it, the temperature, the sound it makes. Give it your whole attention, the way the yogis gave theirs to the breath. If your mind wanders off to the next job, bring it back to this one. If you pray, you can keep the Name in mind while your hands work. If you don't, the full attention is enough. The bell holds the time.
The true yogi. In Nanak's answer, the Gurmukh, who keeps the Word in ordinary life and stays spotless in the middle of the soot. Today's word.
Your line: yoga in daily life. Today, find the sootiest hour, the busiest or the most irritating, and see if you can stay clear inside it for one minute. Day one thousand one hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Sikh teaching honors the householder's life: Sikhs are encouraged to work, raise families and serve others while keeping the Name, rather than leaving home for the forest.

fork.reveal: the Gurmukh finds the way through the Word, in ordinary life. the soot doesn't disqualify anyone; it's where the practice happens.

original.note: jog: yoga, as the Guru Granth Sahib writes it; jog jugat is the way of yoga.

trapdoor: what you thought: a true yogi lives on a mountain, far from everyone.
what it means: in Nanak's answer the true yogi is the Gurmukh, who keeps the Word in ordinary life.
what a scholar hears: a Suhi hymn of Guru Nanak lists the yogi's outer signs and sets them aside: stay spotless amid the soot.

notes: Suhi Mahala 1 (Ang 730) paraphrased: yoga is not the patched coat, the staff, ashes, earrings, a shaven head or blowing the horn; remaining unstained amid the soot (anjan maahi niranjan raheeai) is how the way of yoga is found. Please confirm paraphrase and Ang.
The script calls the Suhi hymn a summary that 'sits beside' the Sidh Gosht thematically; it is not part of the Sidh Gosht. Please confirm the framing is clear.
Hook says the Siddhs had left homes and families; this follows the Sidh Gosht's framing of them as renunciants. Please confirm.
Original ਜੋਗੁ (jog) as written in Gurbani; please confirm spelling and pronunciation guide.
